In reality, most communities are filled with well-meaning adults who are willing to help a child who is lost, hurt, or scared.

As children in my city transition to walking or biking to school and around their neighborhoods independently—often between 3rd and 5th grade, and almost entirely by middle school—the greatest threat to their safety is not strangers, but automobile traffic.

If you're concerned about the welfare of children in America, the most impactful action you can take is to drive slower and remain undistracted. Adhering to lower speed limits in cities, such as the 20 mph standard proposed by global safety initiatives, directly saves lives. Please drive slower at all times, stay attentive, and share the road responsibly to keep our kids safe.

The companies like UPS that employ the model have greater control over the work and the employees, and therefore their brand. The contractor model used by companies like FedEx and Amazon gives the company greater flexibility, allows them to scale quicker using less capital because subcontractors invest their own money in equipment, and some liability benefits. If NYC bans companies from using delivery subcontractors, the cost of delivery will go up and the number of delivery jobs will go down. Who would think that government intervention in the market would reduce jobs and raise prices?

He was the king, for goodness sake. We know that Henry the eighth was actually Henry Tudor. But I have never heard him referred to as Tudor.

This is not something I am going on about in some sort of silly way. I think it is blatant evidence of something ridiculous that is going on. I think there is a modern unwillingness to accept old ways, perhaps old ways of respect or custom.

I was a commercial builder in my career, often responsible for tall and / or big projects. I have a lot of confidence in the design teams, design review teams and inspectors, insofar as code compliance is the issue. But some of big disasters, like the Kansas City Hyatt walkways collapse, were caused by failures to execute the approved plans. We all heard about the walkways collapse and many people know they were caused by a change made to the plans to make execution easier. At least in this case a change was requested by the builder and approved at a low level by the structural engineer who didn’t appreciate that this change entirely negated the integrity of his design. But fewer people know that the builder didn’t correct a buckled roof deck and ended up filling it with several feet of concrete instead of the 4” called for. Few people know that the strucural glass wall installed at the entry was not anchored at its base when the contractor deceptively installed anchor nuts that appeared to be threaded on anchor bolts  that actually.

Other times the overall system worked great, like after the Nothridge earthquake, when a failed weld was discovered (by an observant janitor!) that left the building within a few seconds of shaking long enough to collapse. The teams of engineers that travel to earthquakes to assess design codes immediately recognized that a catastrophe had been narrowly avoided in lots of similar buildings. They immediately changed the welding code.

This article touches all too briefly on the internet role in changing the way we perceive the truth.

Unlike the human brain, the internet does not forget anything. As a result, it is increasingly full of information that cannot be trusted. As Harari tells it, “The problem is in our information. Humans, yes, we are generally good and wise, but if you give good people bad information, they make bad decisions.”

This internet was designed to provide reliable end-to-end communication, to make a best effort to deliver that information in spite of failures of network nodes and transmission facilities. The designer's altruistic intentions were to connect remote researches to data that was difficult to find and retrieve.

Then commercial interests took over and gave us "social networking," exposing millions of us to divisive viewpoints. Unfortunately, our reptilian brains were aroused. Our visceral reactions were amplified by algorithms of the social network. The social network has made us into addicts. I call it "digital dopamine." Our reward system has been hacked, and the social network has become our jailer.

We no longer have privacy and safety. Human beings were designed to survive in times of peril. Now we are fearful all of the time. The safeguards of distance and defensive barriers of "civilization" have been breached, all in the name of freedom of speech.

 Anyone can yell "fire" in a crowded theater. I challenge you to propose a technical solution to this problem.

Aside from the intangible magic of the composer's actual handwriting, these original scores, for me, inspire awe at the labor required to produce a large score  (or, simply stay alive) in the pre-modern world. Every note, every dot, every letter, was written by hand.   In a room with no electric light, no indoor plumbing, no running water.   No car to drive to a rehearsal. No email to distribute the score.  No phone to talk with anyone about what you have written.  My god, how did they have time?

And yet, Mahler wrote mind-bending symphonies, in a matter weeks, with no way to hear what they actually sounded like until played.  Now, any yo yo (including me--I'm an avid amateur) can write music on a computer program, play it back one second later, email it to a colleague or performer, and edit it repeatedly, effortlessly.  With nary a thought about the demands of daily life: food, transport, poop.  

We take this all for granted because it's our life, and we can scarcely imagine it any other way.  But looking at a Mahler score reminds me that none of our modern comforts are essential.  It's Mahler that's essential, and he needed none of our tools to produce his astonishing music.

The new Lumipulse G pTau217/ß-Amyloid 1-42 Plasma Ratio test described in the article is only FDA approved for adult patients, aged 55 years and older, ALREADY exhibiting signs and symptoms of the disease. Why are people getting the Lumipulse test before showing cognitive decline?

Everyone with Alzheimer's has been shown to have amyloids in the brain during autopsies. BUT there also also many cognitively normal people with amyloids in their brains during autopsies. 

The only currently FDA approved Alzheimer's drug therapies are for Amyloid removal, but these are therapies with side effects. So the Lumipulse is useful as one screening tool if these therapies are being considered to treat measured cognitive decline. But without any measured cognitive decline, what is the point of taking the Lumipulse test? Again, there are plenty of autopsies of cognitively normal people that show amyloids.

Once again, and to be emphatic:
There is NO cure for Alzheimer’s.

There is NO definitive test for Alzheimer’s.

Alzheimer’s medication may or may not work. Alzheimer’s treatments are such that those  purporting to slow progression or more are simply educated guesses or cruel hoaxes. Progress cannot be measured because Alzheimer’s itself  plateaus, rapidly progresses, slows down, and defy whatever scientific method is applied. 
 
People say they want to “know” to settle their affairs. But this skips the part where there is no knowing because a supposedly positive result is inconclusive until it is not.

My wife and I experienced 3 out of 4 parents succumbing to Alzheimer’s. My dad died of other complications before it overcame him. He was the “fortunate “ one. None of them progressed the same. None of them had the same lifespan after doctors gave their diagnostic guesses. My MIL suffered for over 20 years. My mom and FIL far less, yet different. Doctors have no answer. We grew to understand and accept this. What do we do? We live our best lives as we are able. We are healthy and refuse to dwell on what might be. This can take over your life if allowed. 

This is not to say progress is not being made. It is. There is significant research into Alzheimer’s. But there is a huge difference between progress and cure. I’m not blaming doctors. A fair doctor will tell you the truth, no mumbo jumbo. Demand honesty.

In the UK, it’s being heavily promoted across the media as a thrilling experience, even though it will be, at best, a 95% partial eclipse. I’m sure the journalists promoting it are well meaning, but as someone who experienced a total eclipse far out at sea in 1999, I can tell you that the difference between 100% and even 99% is quite literally night and day.

It’s like being in a completely dark room (or an airplane cabin) and someone lifts the blackout blind by just a sliver — suddenly, the room is flooded with light. That final 1% makes an extraordinary difference.

100% totality is the key. During the 1999 eclipse, I watched what I call the “black monster” advancing towards me across the ocean. As it arrived, the midday sky darkened, the stars appeared, and then came Bailey’s Beads. It was utterly astonishing and magnificent.

And then, just a few seconds after totality ended, the sky was flooded with light again and the magic was gone.

So while a 95% partial eclipse will undoubtedly be an impressive sight, it really isn’t the same experience as totality. Until you’ve witnessed that final fraction of a percent disappearing, it’s almost impossible to appreciate just how dramatic the difference is.

Last year I booked a holiday in southern Spain, for August 2027 to witness the “eclipse of the century” and I’m giddy at the thought of experiencing totality once again.  It really is the most awe-inspiring thing you will ever see.

There was always tons of inventory and initial orders were very large.  The benefits to the retailers was better pricing. The factories were always busy and the consumer got their goods on time every time throughout the season (back to school, holiday, Christmas etc.) and prices were reasonable for consumers too.  Our family apparel business had 9 factories in New York and PA.  We did work for Sears, Penny's, Bloomies and the rest all year. LW3

Feeling ghosted is hard. You just want to know what went wrong and wonder if you can repair it. 

Most ghosting is because of immature people who don’t know how to have an uncomfortable conversation.  

But *some* ghosting is because the person is overwhelmed with life. It’s not because of you. They just don’t know how to deal with all the moving parts in their life right now and are withdrawing from others.  

This can be because of overwhelming commitments, personal tragedy, or even abusive relationship. There can be a lot of shame in ghosting other people when you get overwhelmed with life. 

My suggestion is one last message along the lines of *“Hey, I haven’t heard from you in a while. I’m guessing you’ve got a lot going on right now. We have all been there. When things change feel free to reach out. It would be nice to reconnect.”*

If the other person is just being immature, this won’t accomplish much. But if the other person is overwhelmed, this message leaves the door open for someone who is ashamed of how they treated you to get back in touch. 

Good luck in life. It’s a grand adventure.

My sympathies go out to everyone affected by this event. No mention here though of the depth of the epicentre.

In my experience, this is an important factor. As a general rule, deep quakes are felt over a wide area, but cause limited damage for their strength; shallow quakes are felt locally and do substantial damage, relatively.

An example: I clearly remember a quake of 7.0 in Ecuador that went on for ages. I went upstairs, came back down again and doors and furniture were still swinging gently. The epicentre was around 100 miles north of us and at a depth of over 70 miles. It was felt everywhere in the country and one wall toppling was the only damage reported. Meanwhile, there was a tremor of just 4 in Murcia, Spain around the same time that caused a load of damage, with a depth of 1 km.

The depth of this one is reported elsewhere at around 107 km (65 miles), so I am not surprised it was felt over a wide area. There will surely be some questions about the quality of the buildings though. No one should really be surprised at earthquakes to the west of the Andes, so it is sad that such damage occurred.
